The [b]Enginner[/b], for example, can launch a clay-mold and form a platform near a mineral, which then the [b]Scout[/b] can hook into to harvest materials quickly. It makes for a focus-point on teamwork and working as a unit.

The classes keep the game enjoyable for a while, but the mission objectives dampers the experience. At first, they are stable but become dull in no time as you realize that once you played a couple of hours, you have seen almost all of them. If there was more variety to them in further updates, I think that would make the game shine even more than it already does.

[h1]For Karl!!! [/h1]
There are a lot of side-diversions that are fun to watch and participate in it, drinking beer that makes you pass out or jump while exploding, throwing barrels into a platform to score points (or throw yourself into) and dancing floor with wild music. I had a lot of joy and laughs with them and would look forward to doing them after a mission! Unlocking new beers is exciting and inviting rounds on fellow players so that they can experience the effects and have a sense of brotherhood and camaraderie.

Due to the lack of missions, as stated in the previous segment, the game can become repetitive, which can lean to you getting burned out of it, as I did. If you are not into repetition, you might want to consider whenever this is for you or not.

[h1]Drop pod will leave with or without you.[/h1]
Combat is one of the best parts of [b]Deep Rock Galatic![/b] Shooting the bugs (mostly spiders) with the different weapons that you can personalize to your style with mods and overclock is satisfactory! Several types of enemies will make their way to you as you explore the caves, ranging from killer robots that will melt rocks to parasites underground or wasps-like creatures trying to kidnap you! You must fulfill your objectives and then escape into the pod or risk imminent dead miner.

Solo-play is one of the things that I didn't have fun with when playing this game. Is directed towards being a multiplayer experience. Whenever with randoms or friends you can have a lot of fun with other players. In contrast, playing solo feels tedious as you are completing objectives at a snail pace, and it's rather monotonous. I only suffered this during the tutorial, which is understandable, and during a [b]Deep Dive[/b], I failed just seconds before beating the mission. I couldn't find a session for endgame content as promptly as the core content.

[h1] Strong and Weak Points[/h1]
The strong point in this game is that there is a lot of distinct zones to explore and that they have their unique hazards from frozen worlds with glaciers to deserts with sandstorms or hard rock flowing with lava. They have their distinct artistic surroundings in addition to the dangers they present. You spend as much time battling the creatures as you fight the planet: falling in a pit mid-combat, getting burned alive, or being stuck in place by the cold as enemies bite into you, they are dangerous places.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2132350301

The weak point here is the durability of the title. Featuring up to 6-8 hours of content, it is of grinding and replayability nature. Is it a pleasure during that time, but if you are firmly against playing the same missions always, you might get bored out of it in no time. There is endgame content known as the [b]Deep Divers[/b] that are three-stage objectives, yet it takes a while to get to them, and after it, there is not much to do that is fresh. If you, for example like [b] Left for Dead 2[/b] or [b]Warhammer Vermintide 2[/b] go for it, but if you don't, consider not buying this game.

[h1] Rock and Stone!!![/h1]
The caves in the [b]Deep Rock Galatic[/b] are intricated mazes that follow a complex structure. You are free to decide how you will transverse them as you move forward, and depending on your approach; they can be simple or a headache. It is fascinating, as I explore caves in different fashions depending on the objectives, my class, and the terrain. 

However, there is a learning curve in getting to know how to take the best approach. During my first hours with the game, I would easily get lost in these well-designed tombs that can certainly trap you in. It gets better with time, but you must be ready to adapt to the planet quickly or suffer the consequences. I recommend sticking with teammates during your first couple of missions until you get the hang of it. Both the [b]Scout[/b] and [b]Gunner[/b] are a lot of fun to play as and easy to move around.

[h1]X Notes[/h1]
I run the game on a GTX 1060 and an RTX 2070 S. There were no issues in any of the cards. Weapons have multiple mods to get modified with, and there are beers to unlock with licenses. Beer effects can be comedic or affect gameplay with bonuses as additional health or the ability to instantly destroy rocks with your pickaxe. Some bosses are hard to defeat but exciting encounters, and you can even recruit some of them temporarily should you beat them!

Classes are straight but have more depth build into them than at first glance. For example, you can play an [b]Engineer[/b] and think that all you do is shoot, build turrets, and make stairs or bridges with the clay. However, if you are ingenious, you realize that enemies are coming from the ceiling. You can use your clay to fill those holes, making enemies take longer detours or altogether from spamming near your team, and that is a fantastic experience. Be sure to experiment with the classes to have a phenomenal time!

[h1] Finally…[/h1]
[b]Deep Rock Galatic[/b] is an amazing title. It has a lot of quality build into it, and the developers have put a lot of care into their project. If you want to have fun, do grab it! Situations can be as absurd as falling 1000 meters to your death or getting strapped to a drill and going outside the map (happened to a scout I played with). I recommend this to anyone except those that dislike repetitive objectives and missions. Have fun in the caves, and if you like this review, give it a thumbs up! Deep Rock Galactic* and the 500 Lives I Saved: A Journey from Pixels to Reality

There are moments in life when a game transcends entertainment and becomes something more profound—something that shapes your actions and changes your perspective. For me, that game was *Deep Rock Galactic*. It’s not just a co-op, sci-fi, mining, and combat game; it’s where I learned the value of teamwork, sacrifice, and the kind of grit that extends beyond the digital universe. Little did I know that playing this game would eventually lead me to saving the lives of 500 homeless people. I know, it sounds insane, but let me explain.

It all started innocently enough. A few friends and I were looking for something to do together, something cooperative and fun. After a couple of rounds of various games, we stumbled across *Deep Rock Galactic*—a game where you play as a team of dwarves sent into deep, alien caves to mine valuable resources. There’s a catch, though: the caves are crawling with dangerous creatures, and the mission is dangerous from the moment you step inside. But what really drew me in was the camaraderie—four dwarves, working together, each with different skills, facing impossible odds in the pursuit of profit.

At first, it was all fun. The game was an exhilarating mix of combat, resource gathering, and working as a team to stay alive. There were moments of chaos, moments of triumph, and moments of failure. As a team, we’d get overwhelmed by alien swarms or buried in the depths of the cave, our way out blocked by shifting terrain. We learned quickly that *Deep Rock Galactic* wasn’t about playing solo—it was about relying on your teammates, each dwarf’s skills complementing the others’. Without communication and trust, the whole mission would fail. 

But as I spent more time playing the game, something unexpected started to happen. It wasn’t the game mechanics or the addictive loop of mining and shooting that started to stick with me—it was the *feeling* of teamwork and purpose. Each mission in *Deep Rock Galactic* was about making it to the extraction point alive, ensuring that everyone had what they needed to survive, and that no dwarf was left behind. It was about sacrifice—doing whatever it took to protect your crew, even if it meant putting yourself in danger.

I didn’t know it at the time, but this mindset would change everything for me.

One weekend, while playing with my friends, I found myself reflecting on what I was really doing with my life. I’d been in a rut for a while—working long hours at a desk job that drained me, living in a city that felt increasingly detached and impersonal. I had no real sense of purpose outside of work and gaming. It wasn’t until I found myself in one of those high-pressure *Deep Rock Galactic* missions, where the whole team was about to fail, that I had this strange moment of clarity. I was working with my team to fight off hordes of enemies and trying to clear a path to the extraction point, and in that moment, it hit me: **If we could band together to survive in this game, why couldn’t we do something similar in real life? Why couldn’t we come together to help people in need?**

The thought stayed with me for days, gnawing at my conscience. I was sitting comfortably at home, playing with my friends, while others in the world—people struggling with homelessness—had no such luxury. They were stuck in real-life caves, in a sense—trapped in situations that felt impossible to escape. It was a stark realization: **I had a chance to make a difference, to be part of something bigger than just my own comfort.**

I couldn’t shake it. The idea of rescue, the idea of *saving* people from their own alien-like cave, took root in my mind. And like any good mission in *Deep Rock Galactic*, it needed a plan. I began researching local shelters, talking to people involved in homelessness outreach, and trying to figure out how I could take action. I wanted to be a part of the solution, not just a bystander in the face of such overwhelming need. I began to understand that helping people wasn’t just about writing a check or volunteering on occasion—it was about building a system of support, about pulling people out of the metaphorical caves and providing them with the tools and resources they needed to survive, thrive, and ultimately escape their situation.

Soon, I was in contact with several local non-profits. At first, I helped organize fundraisers and drive supplies. But as I got more involved, I realized that my work wasn’t just about giving material resources—it was about creating lasting change, about restoring dignity and hope. I wanted to offer more than just handouts; I wanted to help build a community where homeless people could get the help they needed, whether it was shelter, mental health services, job training, or simply a hand to pull them out of the depths they were trapped in.

The more time I spent helping, the more I realized how much the analogy to *Deep Rock Galactic* applied. Homelessness, in many ways, was a game where survival was the ultimate goal, and each person needed a team to survive. A team of people who were willing to fight alongside them, no matter how dark or dangerous the environment. And like the dwarves in the game, I began to see that no one should be left behind.

I decided to make it my personal mission to rescue 500 people from homelessness in my city. It wasn’t easy. There were countless setbacks—shelters full to capacity, bureaucracy that slowed progress, and the harsh reality of how deep the problem went. But each small success kept me going, kept me motivated. I spent hours organizing events, building partnerships with local businesses to create job opportunities, and advocating for policies that would provide more affordable housing. I poured everything I had into it. The same teamwork and resolve that I had learned from playing *Deep Rock Galactic* became my guiding principles. **Rescue wasn’t just about completing a mission. It was about lifting others up, making sure no one got left behind, and working together to break through barriers.**

Eventually, I reached my goal: 500 people helped off the streets and into safe environments where they could start rebuilding their lives. These weren’t just numbers to me—they were lives saved, families reunited, individuals who had been lost in the system now given the chance for a future. It felt like we had fought our way through the worst of the alien infested caves, and now we had our hands on the precious resources they so desperately needed to survive.

In the end, *Deep Rock Galactic* wasn’t just a game I played for fun—it was a catalyst that inspired me to take action, to use the values of teamwork, sacrifice, and perseverance to make a tangible impact in the world. The feeling of pulling together, rescuing my fellow dwarves from danger, eventually turned into the motivation to rescue real people, helping them out of the caves of homelessness and into a better future. 

If anything, I learned that games can teach us more than we think—especially when we realize that sometimes, the most important missions aren’t the ones we complete on the screen. Sometimes, the real mission is saving lives. And sometimes, it all starts with a game that teaches you to fight for those who can’t fight for themselves.

[h1]Early Access review, based on Update 21.[/h1]

[b]TL;DR This game is Vermintide meets Minecraft[/b]

[u]Gameplay Story[/u]
We had just finished our objective on the Crystalline Caverns - kill 3 of the biggest, meanest bugs this hostile planet has to offer. We loaded up our robotic mine cart full of extra goods we'd found along the way, and called for an extract.

The drop pods plops down on the other side of the maze of caves we'd traversed to, and calling it had prompted the hostile bugs to find a new source of minions to throw at us - we didn't have time to snake our way back and risk getting lost, so our Driller starts cutting through the stone and begins creating a tunnel straight to the pod, on an incline. 

The bugs followed closely behind, and began to pour into the tunnel like water filling a glass. I, the Gunner, began emptying lead into the formless mass of chitin and teeth. The Engineer was plopping down their sentry turrets to help me stem the tide. The Scout was doing what they could to throw 'slow' grenades to help slow the feckers down. Every bullet we had [i]just wasn't enough, they kept coming![/i]. Eventually the Driller broke through into the area where the pod was sitting, waiting, but it's doors were closed; We had to hold the tunnel until our M.U.L.E loaded up into the pod before we could actually leave.

The Driller pulled out his flamethrower to join us, and turned the tunnel into hell itself. Some of the big, lumbering, acid-spitting, brainless and armoured bugs were slowly thundering through the tunnel and were shrugging off most of our bullets from the front. We chucked nades and projectiles at 'em to slow them down.

By this point we were nearly out of ammo, and 'Molly' (affectionately named) finished taking her long way round route to get into the pod. With yells of "Rock and Stone!" we loaded up as the last of the big bastards spat its acid at our heels. I had around 100 rounds left on my minigun, and the others were nearly dry too - but we made it, and the payday was ours.

------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

[b]This is just a taste of the gameplay DRG has to offer[/b]. Half the time, you are just exploring and mining. It's casual, and reminiscent of spelunking in Minecraft. You find a vein here or there and dig away, occasionally calling your 'M.U.L.E' to drop off the ore you are carrying. Sometime you find veins that are out of reach, and need to creatively work together to get those precious resources. Then, the call comes in over your comms. 

[i]"Swarm! I repeat, SWARM![/i]. The music swells and out of every nook and cranny bugs pour out and attempt to overwhelm and devour you. You switch to combat mode, hopefully forming up to take them down together, or risk fighting alone and getting brought down in the darkness.

DRG finds a happy middle ground between these two styles of gameplay and the two work wonders together. You don't get bored mining because before long, a group of enemies are around to harass you. You don't get [i]too[/i] stressed fighting (usually, harder difficulties change this) because you fight to get that breathing room to relax and mine again. 

I recommend this game even in it's current state. There is character progression, and each class feels different enough to warrant their own 'role' in the game. There is variety in the map types and I don't get bored doing the somewhat similar missions over and over because I am compelled to reach that next payday to unlock the next item to play with. 

It's stable, optimised, and most of all very fun. I play with and without friends and I have mostly found that randoms are friendly and help out. Join the DRG company and I'll buy you a pint, and wish you a warm [b]"Rock and Stone - [i]to the bone[/i]"[/b]

The Game is built around PvE Coop with 4 classes: The Gunner, the Engineer, the Driller and the Scout. The names are a bit misleading though, since they all can fight and they all have defensive or offensive capabilities. The Gunner has a big gun but so does the Engineer with his grenade launcher while the Driller has the Flamethrower to go full Ellen Ripley on the monsters. Each class has different unique skills though. The Engineer can put up plattforms and has a sentry to put up,, the Gunner has ziplines to make it look like the ski lifts in the alps and his shield protects everybody, combine both though and you can zipline to a platform to mine otherwise unreachable minerals. The Driller, as the name implies has 2 massive drills to go through mountains like they're butter. The Scout has a zipline. which works well with the Engineers platforms, sadly his weapons are kinda weak and also sadly, most people playing him ignore his flares, so while he is supposed to light up caves, rarely anybody actually does it.  

Next to the Aliens the missions are filled with dangers, steep drops, rough terrain, nuclear diamonds and poison mushrooms that release so much green smoke not even Mario would want to eat them, as well as spikes, spit throwing plants and random nature catastrophes like sand/icestorms (that make you blind or freeze you) or earthquake that rip apart the earth, so you might even fall to your death or onto lava to burn. Remember that stupid "The floor is lava" meme? It's coming to reality in this game in one biome, where you have to parcour around burning terrain.

The Aliens also come in all forms and f fashions. Harmless small things that gnaw on your dwarfy legs to flying enemies that zap you to plants on the ceiling that grab you (Totally not stolen from Half-Life) to Sandworms that take you for an unwelcome ride (Totally not stolen from Dune) or big monstrosities that explode or spit stuff at you.

Missions range so far from simple mining operations (mine 2 kinds of stuff) to Elimination (Eliminate several Glyphid Dreadnought and yes, they sound as nasty as the name implies) to Point Extraction (get stuff to a mining plattform), Egg Hunt (steal alien eggs, which unleashes a terrifying cry of pain and usually a swarm of aliens) and Salvage Operation, where you clean up the mess a previous dwarven crew left (they died, they fucked up, their mules are broken, repair them, repair their pod, try to escape)
Since mission types only would be a bit boring and Mutators have been popular since at least UT99, we get them as well, randomly, on missions. They can be either really good (like lots more gold, lots more minerals, weak hitpoints on aliens) or really bad (no 02, so you run out of air and have to stick to the mule or drop pod, enemies that spawn smaller enemies when they die or the nastiest thing ever: haunted caves, where a Bulk Detonator plays Predator, goes mostly invisible, haunts you, is invincible and can fuck an entire team in 40 seconds)
Once you survived all that, you can jump into Deep Dive missions, that are even more dangerous and more difficult. 

Now to fight all this nasty stuff, you of course can upgrade your dwarf with more skills and perks, both active and passive, as well as promote him to get another passive/active perk. Promoting a class at least once is basically needed once you go beyond Hazard 3 (out of 5)
You can go Solo and either you have an (upgradable) flying Bot named Bosco with you, who you can somewhat control to mine minerals or shoot rockets at enemies (otherwise it just flies around and uses 2 guns to shoot at stuff, as well as being able to revive you a limited numer of times) but this game certainly is a ton more fun with other people who play all roles or at least most roles 

What else is there to say: Graphically it's nothing special but the terraforming maps are the best since Red Faction, which basically really introduced it in 2001. You can dig, mine, bomb your way around and discover hidden events, hidden loot and dead  dwarves to get cosmetics (yes, we don't just drink and mine, we also rob the dead!). 
The sound is a bit mixed. The music is great altough some pieces totally sound like they were stolen straight from Mass Effect, but the new stuff is great, even though again it takes inspiration from several things like the Abyss, but it's more diverse. The effects are good, the grenade launcher makes enough noise to keep a subwoofer happy. The voices are, limited. 1 guy voices all characters with just differences in pitch and you can easily tell, that gives them a bit less personality compared to other PvE games like Payday or Vermintide where the different voice actors make the characters shine - and after a while you wanna shut down the command guy who sounds all smarty pants and acts like he actually launches the swarms at you and is surprised you survived them.He is an asshole.
But that's basically my only criticism, I really would like to have different voice actors for the dwarves.

What needs to be noticed is: NO Microtransactions. Some DLC with a Soundtrack, a Supporter Pack that only features gaudy (gold) cosmetics and two cosmetic packs (see my reviews on those for my oppinion), that only add skins but nothing that changes the gameplay or gives you an advantage. So you don't need to buy these unless you really want to support the ongoing development of this game. 

There's also some entertainment for the hardworking dwarves in the form of barrels you can kick around, an actually barrel kicking mini game, the always great juke box where you can dance and most importantly: Beer. There are beers that just get you drunk, beers that put a variety of fun effects on you (like sending you to some random spot, make you fart or set you on fire) and the daily brews that give you a boost for the next mission, wether it's having some more pickaxe power, giving your more health or the always awesome pot o' gold beer that doubles your gold in take, so you can become the richest dwarf in the galaxy.

Anyway, if you can't tell: This game is absolutely awesome and a blast to play. The community is mostly nice enough, with everybody just having fun and rarely any idiots, griefers or trolls (though some exist but so far not nearly as much as in any other online game i play).

[b] This game is absolutely excellent, one of the best co-op games I have ever experienced after decades of gaming. [/b]

[b] Premise of the game: [/b]
You are a dwarf working for Deep Rock Galactic, a space mining conglomerate that has about as much concern for your safety as a 19th century coal mining company. Your team's job is to plunge into the depths of Hoxxes IV, kill bugs, extract resources and get out before the escape pod leaves you behind to be consumed by the local fauna.

[b] Genre: [/b]
Cooperative first person shooter with mining elements.

[b] Pros: [/b]
[list]
[*]Very polished co-op experience that is a blast to play with friends or a pickup group.
[*]Four very well balanced classes that are both unique and compliment each other.
[*]Playable singleplayer with Bosco, a customizable robotic drone companion with capabilities beyond that of any one of the four dwarf classes.
[*]Perks along with highly customizable weapons and equipment allow a range of unique (and mostly viable) player builds.
[*]Great sense of humor.
[*]Ruthlessly intense action on higher difficulty levels.
[*]Procedurally generated caves that do a mostly good job of appearing unique every game.
[*]Public multiplayer community with a very low level of toxicity. 
[*][u]Zero microtransactions[/u], cosmetic items are purchasable with in-game currency only.
[*]The art style and graphics look great and complement the game without compromising performance.
[*]Fully destructible terrain.
[*]Mining mechanics are fun and lend the game a bit of a Minecraft vibe alongside the dangerous, procedurally generated caves.
[*]Live "Space Rig" lobby gives your team something to do while you wait for the host or an AFK teammate.
[*]Open multiplayer games are drop-in/drop-out, difficulty scales with the player count. No need to wait for a full lobby, no worries if someone has to split.
[/list]

[b] Cons: [/b]
[list]
[*]Some (very few) procedural elements of caves are too unique and will be noticed when they have been seen a few times.
[*]End-game weapon upgrades are relatively new (as of the writing of this review) and can be anywhere from underwhelming to overpowered.
[*]Mission and environment variety has been fine for me, but I can see some folks getting bored around the 100 hour mark, the devs plan to expand this.
[*]Availability of special resources (used for upgrading your kit and buying cosmetics) could use a little balancing. 
[/list]

[b] Performance: [/b]
[list]
[*]I am playing this game on a GTX 1070 Ti at 1440p, with 16 gigs of DDR4 and an i7 8700K - this game has had [i]zero[/i] performance issues for me at max settings. Edit: Updating to state that I do see some FPS drops at high difficulty with a full team (large numbers of bugs spawned in, don't think it's client-side opposed to internet/host issues.) 
[*]Should be able to be played with acceptable performance on most potato PCs. 
[*]Very low prevalence of bugs, mostly revolving around newly introduced features.
[/list]

[b] Other notes: [/b]
[list]
[*]As of the writing of this review this game is at the tail end of its Early Access development.
[*]Built in VOIP.
[*]Despite some mild swearing, this game is pretty kid friendly. Naturally, their mileage may vary in public multiplayer.
[*]Pausable in singleplayer.
[*]Short mission length (generally 30-60 minutes) means the game can be easily picked up and put down.
[*]Games are player hosted which means the host is always the admin. There is no messing with votekick or other weak multiplayer mechanics. With the exception of the occasional bad host, this means trolls and griefers are nipped in the bud easily.
[*]Being a locally hosted, non-competitive, coop single/multiplayer game the devs do not actively counter hackers. Hackers can modify rewards, so if you don't want your game's progression compromised, do not stay in a hacker's server!
[*]This game is unapologetically masculine - this game is literally about a bunch of manly dwarves killing bugs, breaking rocks and slamming back brews. That's refreshing given the past few years of AAA devs trying to check boxes in video games. Sorry, not sorry. 
[/list]

[b] Value: [/b]
This game is priced fairly, and is [i]easily[/i] worth full price at $30. It does go on sale down to $20 from time to time.

[b] This game is truly one of the best co-op FPS yet, and is a great example of Early Access done right! [/b]

Danger. Darkness. Dwarves.

So lets cover each key point there.

1) Danger.

Me and my miner friends thought to ourselves "Hey we've played these games a hundred times." and jumped into a mission one difficulty level higher than standard. This turned out to be the worst decision we had ever made as our drill drop pod opened itself to a scene from Starship Troopers. 
Our scout ziplined away to the other side of the cave where he was spit on by web slinging bugs and exploded thanks to a nearby suicide bug, our driller ran to the nearest wall and drilled himself a dead end grave whilst screaming the entire time over voice chat, our gunner fired his minigun from the doorway as I (the engi) tried to get turrets up just in time to take down the Patrician bug coming up the ramp which then released gas into the entire spawn chamber on death forcing us to leave right in to a chasm where one of us went down to fall damage. 

Then the drop pod left.

This game has danger.

2) Darkness.

This game is DARK, this game is the kind of game where you see your allies have torches on their armour and say "Hey, how do you turn the torch on?" only to find your torch was already on and you've made the situation oh so much worse.

You can call in a Floodlight to light up big open cave areas you've dug in to, but it costs gold so you better have mined some. You can also call in a giant sentry gun, which is handy when you're suddenly told a swarm is coming. But not so handy if you want to use that gold for a floodlight.

3) Dwarves.

This game is a Dwarf game. It's as simple as that. If you dream of gold, if you dream of digging and delving, if your beard is longer than your hair then this is exactly the game you're on this page to find. Greed and Gold are king here and you'll go back into another nightmare soley because you want more credits to upgrade your gear. I've never seen a better execution of what it means to be a dwarf in a sci-fi setting.

You dig, you mine, you make money, you call the driller a whale-piper for drilling into you by mistake and you yell "DONKEY!" for a box on legs to come and let you drop in your hard earned gold... And then you probably die, holding as much minerals as you can, surrounded by stone. The dream.



Play this game. Buy it. Win a key, Enter a competition, Beg your mother for a copy. Whatever you need to do to get this game. If you have 3 friends and you like screaming in deep dark pits as everything goes to hell. Play it.

Deep Rock Galactic is one of those rare games where everything just clicks — the gameplay, the vibe, the community, and most importantly, the devs behind it. If you’ve ever wanted to go on chaotic space mining missions with your friends while fending off alien bugs and yelling “ROCK AND STONE!” every five minutes, this is your calling.

The core gameplay is simple but endlessly fun: you’re a dwarf in space, you mine valuable materials, you fight off waves of hostile creatures, and you GTFO before it all collapses. But it’s how the game feels that makes it special. Each class plays differently and contributes in unique ways, so whether you’re drilling through rock, setting up turrets, lighting up the cave, or ziplining across a chasm, you always feel useful — and the teamwork is real.

The environments are fully destructible and randomly generated, which keeps things fresh. Sometimes you’re zipping through caves like a pro, and other times you’re lost, surrounded, and yelling for your engineer to PLEASE set up a platform. It’s tense, hilarious, and incredibly satisfying all at once.

And now — the devs. Ghost Ship Games is one of the best dev teams in the industry, period.
They didn’t just launch a great game and walk away — they’ve been updating Deep Rock Galactic consistently with free content, new missions, weapons, cosmetics, seasonal events, and quality-of-life changes that actually matter. They listen to feedback, engage with the community, and have built a game that keeps getting better without nickel-and-diming the players.

It’s not just a good co-op game — it’s one of the best.
Whether you’re dropping in solo with your trusty drone, or teaming up with a full squad to shout nonsense while digging your way to glory, DRG delivers every single time. It’s fun, it’s polished, it’s generous, and it has one of the most wholesome, chill communities you’ll find in online gaming.

Buy it. Play it. Shout “Rock and Stone!” unironically. You won’t regret it.

I jumped into Deep Rock Galactic thinking “yeah this looks alright,” and came out shouting ROCK AND STONE like it’s a legally binding greeting.

This game is chaos in the best possible way. You and your friends drop into a cave, immediately get lost, accidentally split up, panic when bugs start pouring out of the walls, and somehow still make it out alive while laughing the whole time. It’s less “tactical mission” and more “dwarven survival comedy.”

The co-op is where it really shines. Every class actually feels useful, so instead of fighting over who gets to be the main character, you’re all just equally responsible for the inevitable disaster. And when things go wrong, they go spectacularly wrong.

And then there’s the bar. Honestly, half my playtime feels like it’s just spent in the Space Rig at the bar, ordering drinks, dancing like absolute idiots, and raising a beer for Karl like true dwarves.

ROCK AND STONE isn’t just a voice line at this point, it’s a lifestyle choice.

Verdict:
🍺 10/10 would mine again
🍺 10/10 would get lost again
🍺 FOR KARL
